# One example, ten chapters

Imagine a small **order-processing service**. A controller submits orders and can request shutdown; a worker consumes published orders; multiple workers later share a processed-order count. The system becomes more demanding as each chapter introduces a new requirement.

We deliberately **keep one Java source file**, [`JmmLab.java`](examples/JmmLab.java), with a single `main(String[] args)`. Each chapter refers to a named method or a nested class in that file.

::: {.callout-tip}
## Get started

Requires a JDK **17 or newer**. The language-law references are based on the official **Java SE 27** specification.

```bash
cd programming-languages/java/jvm/jmm/examples
javac JmmLab.java
java JmmLab all
```

Or run one chapter experiment, e.g. `java JmmLab volatile` or `java JmmLab locks`.

All examples are educational. The deliberately racy plain-field version is discussed but **not** launched as an unbounded spin loop.
:::

## The evolving requirements

| Stage | New problem | Technique added |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | A controller must stop a worker | Shared state and data-race diagnosis |
| 2 | Reason precisely about cross-thread observations | Actions, orders, happens-before, causality |
| 3 | Publish an order and a stop request | `volatile` |
| 4 | Protect order counts and wait for progress | `synchronized`, `wait`, `notifyAll` |
| 5 | Hand off a completed order snapshot | `final`, `CountDownLatch` |
| 6 | Count work from many concurrent workers | `AtomicInteger` |
| 7 | Explore explicit low-level publication ordering | `VarHandle` release/acquire |
| 8 | Choose the correct tool for each production need | Concurrency design patterns |
| 9 | Investigate behaviours systematically | Litmus tests and jcstress |
| 10 | Connect concepts to normative sources | Specification mapping |

## Read the chapters in order

1. [Foundations](01-foundations.qmd) — Why a naive stop flag is not sufficient.
2. [Formal Memory Model](02-formal-model.qmd) — Actions, program order, synchronisation order, happens-before and causality.
3. [Volatile Variables](03-volatile.qmd) — Signal visibility and safely publish ordinary data.
4. [Locks and Synchronisation](04-locks.qmd) — Protect invariants and wait for progress.
5. [Final Fields and Safe Publication](05-final-fields.qmd) — Construct and hand off immutable order records.
6. [Atomicity and Memory Access](06-atomicity.qmd) — Count every processed order without lost increments.
7. [Advanced Memory Ordering](07-advanced-ordering.qmd) — Experiment with `VarHandle` acquire/release.
8. [Practical Concurrency Patterns](08-concurrency-patterns.qmd) — Apply the appropriate primitive.
9. [Experiments and Verification](09-experiments.qmd) — Know what executions do and do not prove.
10. [References and Specification Mapping](10-references.qmd) — Source map, definitions, review.

## Run modes

`plain`, `volatile`, `locks`, `final`, `atomic`, `varhandle`, `lifecycle`, `word-tearing`, `causality`, and `all`.

## An important distinction

The JMM is a **Java language specification about legal interactions through shared memory**. It is not a diagram of a heap, stack, CPU cache, or garbage collector. JVM runtime data areas belong in the separate JVM topic series.
